The run failed because the accepted gate was incompatible with its own containment environment—not because the macOS app failed to build.

| Check | Result | Actual cause |
|---|---|---|
| Release build | Passed | Xcode produced the app successfully. |
| 99-player network | Failed | The gate sandbox denied binding even to `127.0.0.1`: `PermissionError: Operation not permitted`. See [acceptance-progress.jsonl](/Users/gdc/.deadreckon/runstate/task-0-d0f191c7/runs/328a4e34983e61be5dd45e22c9d453db/proofs/acceptance-progress.jsonl:5). |
| Visual comparison | Failed | The frozen verifier has malformed shell quoting. Bash reports a syntax error near line 118; the broken quote starts at [verify_macos_game.sh](/Users/gdc/.deadreckon/jobs/aa49e5aa3f7a460bb574539472c8265d/acceptance/verify_macos_game.sh:109). |

The network failure is deterministic: strict gate evaluation explicitly sets `allow_network: false` in [turn_loop.rs](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-runtime/src/turn_loop.rs:4680), which becomes `(deny network*)` in [commands.rs](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-sandbox/src/commands.rs:439). That denies the verifier’s loopback TCP server at [verify_macos_game.sh](/Users/gdc/.deadreckon/jobs/aa49e5aa3f7a460bb574539472c8265d/acceptance/verify_macos_game.sh:51). The visual check also downloads Nintendo artwork, so it would encounter the same no-network policy after its syntax error was fixed.

Why the agent claimed all checks passed: during turn 1 it edited the workspace copy of the verifier, fixed the quoting and replaced an obsolete macOS capture API. Its modified verifier passed build, the 99-client exchange, and visual comparison in [codex.out](/Users/gdc/.deadreckon/runstate/task-0-d0f191c7/runs/328a4e34983e61be5dd45e22c9d453db/turns/turn-1/codex.out:75). But that modified file had hash `9e252c…`; the approved frozen verifier has hash `6155cf…`. DeadReckon correctly restores `.deadreckon` from trusted lifecycle state before the real gate in [turn_loop.rs](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-runtime/src/turn_loop.rs:6523), so the gate evaluated the original broken verifier.

The UI’s “failed after turn 2” wording is slightly misleading. The gate actually ran after turn 1; turn 2 then produced no deliverable changes, so DeadReckon preserved the previous gate failure. The planner reconstructs the message using the final turn number in [plan.rs](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon/src/commands/plan.rs:4130).

Current status: the screenshot’s run `d7524b52…` has now failed with the exact same two results. Attempt 3, `f515f013…`, started at 22:09:47 EDT and will encounter the same frozen blockers.

The proper correction is outside the child implementation:

- Fix and syntax-check the approved verifier.
- Replace the live Nintendo download with a pinned local fixture.
- Use ScreenCaptureKit instead of `CGWindowListCreateImage`.
- Either permit loopback networking for strict gates or redesign that check not to require TCP.
- Relaunch with a newly approved contract bundle.

I made no changes to the active plan or its files.

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-08-06 02:19:17Z)**_

Yes. DeadReckon is close to supporting this, but the acceptance contract currently does not carry capability requirements into the gate.

Today:

- `AcceptanceCheck` describes only the command and cwd in [gate.rs](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-core/src/gate.rs:140).
- The compiled contract has no capability field in [acceptance.rs](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon/src/commands/acceptance.rs:179).
- Job creation always starts from a networkless `workspace_only` policy in [job.rs](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon/src/commands/job.rs:266).
- The gate independently hardcodes `allow_network: false` in [turn_loop.rs](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-runtime/src/turn_loop.rs:4688).

The right design is to make capabilities an explicit, reviewable part of each done check:

```yaml
version: 2

checks:
  - name: Exercise 99 TCP clients
    kind: shell
    command: bash .deadreckon/acceptance/verify_macos_game.sh network
    capabilities:
      network:
        loopback: true
        outbound: []

  - name: Compare the rendered window
    kind: shell
    command: bash .deadreckon/acceptance/verify_macos_game.sh visual
    capabilities:
      network:
        loopback: false
        outbound: []
```

For external resources, I would avoid live gate networking and declare frozen inputs instead:

```yaml
fixtures:
  - name: tetris-99-reference
    url: https://assets.nintendo.com/example.png
    sha256: "sha256:..."
    destination: .deadreckon/acceptance/fixtures/tetris-99.png
```

The controller downloads and hashes that fixture before approval, displays it in the launch preview, and freezes it into the contract bundle. The gate remains deterministic and offline.

The capability flow should be:

1. The definition-of-done compiler proposes capabilities from the criteria.
2. The operator sees “gate network: loopback” or “external fixtures: 1” before accepting.
3. The approved capabilities are frozen into a new gate-specific section of `JobExecutionPolicy`.
4. The authority digest binds that policy, so it cannot silently escalate later.
5. Gate execution reads the frozen policy instead of hardcoding `allow_network: false`.
6. Each check runs with its minimum capability, and the signed marker records what was granted.

Automatic inference should propose authority, never silently grant it. For example, prose mentioning “99 TCP clients” can propose loopback; arbitrary shell invoking `curl` should fail preflight unless the contract explicitly declares outbound access or a frozen fixture.

For this particular contract, the safest MVP is:

- Add a distinct `loopback` gate capability.
- Keep arbitrary outbound gate networking prohibited.
- Freeze remote comparison assets before launch.
- Run `bash -n` on frozen shell helpers during preflight.
- Add backend tests proving loopback works while internet access remains denied.

That would have rejected this job before it spent any agent turns: one error for malformed Bash, one for undeclared loopback, and one for the unfrozen Nintendo download. No code was changed in this review.
